questions.html:
A lazy programmer thinks that implementing the procedure Merge (of the merge sort) is too complicated. To simplify merge sort he eliminates the merge all together, and only recursively "sorts" the two halves of the array. Here is his pseudo-code.

 

procedure LAZYSORT(A[1..n])
    if n>1 then
        m ←⌊n/2⌋
        LAZYSORT(A[1..m])
        LAZYSORT(A[m+1..n])

Which of the following is/are TRUE about LAZYSORT?

options.html: The Time Complexity of LAZYSORT is $\theta(n \log n)$
LAZYSORT changes the original array in such a way that it exchanges the first half of the array with the second half.
LAZYSORT does not change array elements at all

questions.solution:
Answer: B, D

questions.html: Consider a constant $\alpha = 0.3$. If we use randomized quick sort (pivot chosen is uniform random) then what is the probability that the partition method will result in an array such that the size of the smaller subarray is $\geq \alpha n$ where $n$ is the total size of the array?

Consider a quicksort where splits at every level are in the proportion of $\alpha$, which means one of the partitions is $\alpha n$ and the other partition is $(1-\alpha) n$. The recursive equation of time complexity can be written as

$$T(n)=T(\alpha n)+T(1-\alpha) n)+n.$$ Consider a recursion tree of function calls and let $x$ be the height of the tree when we hit the base case the first time and let $y$ be the maximum height of the tree then, which of the following is/are true?
Base case is an array containing single element.

options.html: $\alpha^ x n=1$ and $(1-\alpha)^ y n=1$ if $\alpha<0.5$
$\alpha^ y n=1$ and $(1-\alpha)^ x n=1$ if $\alpha<0.5$
$\alpha^ x n=1$ and $(1-\alpha)^ y n=1$ if $\alpha>0.5$
$\alpha^ y n=1$ and $(1-\alpha)^ x n=1$ if $\alpha>0.5$

questions.solution:
Answer: A, D

Suppose you are given $k$ sorted arrays, each with $n$ elements, and you want to combine them into a single array of kn elements. Consider the following approach. Divide the $k$ arrays into $k / 2$ pairs of arrays, and use the Merge subroutine of MergeSort to combine each pair. Now you are left with $k / 2$ sorted arrays, each with $2 n$ elements.

Repeat this approach until you have a single sorted array with kn elements. What is the running time of this procedure, as a function of $k$ and $n?$

questions.html:
Consider an array of $n$ distinct integers. An array element is a peak if it is greater than its neighbors.
For corner elements, we need to consider only one neighbor. The corner element is peak only when it's greater than its neighbors.
If there are more than one peak item, simply return one of them.

Example:

  • Input $: [1, 5, 3, 2, 4, 0]$ Output $: 4$
  • Input $: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]$ Output $: 6$
  • Input $: [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2]$ Output $: 7$

We design a divide-and-conquer algorithm that solves this problem. The incomplete pseudo-code is given below.

findPeak(A, i, j){
    if(i==j) //one element
        return i 
    if(i==j-1) //two elements
        if(A[i]> A[j] ) return i
        else return j
    mid = (i+j)/2
    if (A[mid]> A[mid-1] and A[mid]> A[mid+1]) return mid
    if (A[mid-1]> A[mid])
    //line X
    if (A[mid+1]> A[mid])
    //line Y
}

Fill in the blanks for lines $X$ and $Y$.
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B
